title: Control Structures: If‑Else and Loops
summary: This lesson introduces conditional statements and looping constructs that let programs make decisions and repeat actions. Students will learn how to write and use if‑else blocks, while, for, and do‑while loops with clear examples.

sections.heading: If‑Else Statements
sections.body:
An if‑else statement lets a program choose between two paths based on a condition. The condition is a Boolean expression that evaluates to true or false. If the condition is true, the code inside the first block runs; otherwise, the code in the else block runs.

Example: checking a score to decide pass or fail.

sections.heading: Nested If‑Else and Else‑If Chains
sections.body:
Sometimes more than two outcomes are needed. You can nest if statements or use else‑if chains to test multiple conditions in order. The first true condition executes, and the rest are skipped.

This is useful for grading, menu selections, and more.

sections.heading: While Loops
sections.body:
A while loop repeats a block of code as long as a condition remains true. The condition is checked before each iteration, so if it is false at the start, the loop body may never run.

While loops are ideal when you don't know in advance how many times you need to repeat something.

sections.heading: For Loops
sections.body:
A for loop combines initialization, condition, and increment in one line, making it concise for counting loops. It is the most common loop when the number of iterations is known.

You can also use for‑each loops to iterate over arrays or collections.

key_terms.meaning: A Boolean expression that evaluates to true or false, controlling flow.
A statement that executes one block of code if a condition is true, otherwise another block.
A construct that repeats a block of code multiple times.
Repeats while a condition remains true, checking the condition before each iteration.
Repeats a set number of times, with initialization, condition, and increment in one line.
Placing one control structure inside another to handle more complex logic.

quiz.why: The condition x > 5 is false, so the else block runs and prints B.
i starts at 0 and increments until it reaches 4, so the body runs 4 times.

quiz.q: Which loop is best when the number of iterations is known beforehand?
quiz.why: A for loop is designed for a known count of repetitions.

quiz.q: What does the else‑if chain allow you to do?
quiz.why: Else‑if lets you check multiple conditions one after another.

flashcards.back: Executes one block if a condition is true, otherwise another block.
Checked before each iteration; loop may not run at all if false initially.
A control structure placed inside another, e.g., an if inside a while.
Executes the body first, then checks the condition, guaranteeing at least one run.
